doc.title: Tyner McCoy — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

title: African music, dance and Olatunji
summary: Tyner and Aisha recall Philadelphia drummers, his own African and ballet dance study, and Olatunji's Harlem school.

story.theme_name: Playing for dancers: dance bands and the dances themselves
story.community_name: Dancing to the band: quadrilles, waltzes and dance sets

blocks.x: So if we could look at some of the other inspirations and extensions of your music, the other influences, again I was referencing Africa, Sahara, “Man From Tanganyika” although they are, as you said earlier, some direct references to that and direct inspiration, but now you talked about Eric Gravatt having studied African rhythms. Now did you also study African music and if so, what types and how?
Well the thing is, I’m trying to think . . . Saka Eque.
Saka Eque. Yeah you, Saka Eque and Bobby Crowder, yeah they had a good school. Johnny Hines had a dance school and he played conga drums for a while and Garvin Masseaux.
And I studied a little bit of dancing myself. I didn’t want to mention that.
Well please do, that’s important (laughs).
(Laughs) He did.

I did some ballet and African . . . we had some people from Africa that taught African dancing. They needed some male dancers so I volunteered (Aisha and McCoy laugh). [To Aisha ] Well, you could dance that’s the thing, you studied dancing.
Did you all dance together at any point?
I dance with him now (laughs).
Oh OK.
No we didn’t dance together.
See at my age I can’t keep up with her, so it works out fine (laughs) and I won’t embarrass anybody (laughs).
But I think that helped to do the conga drumming. The rhythms, too that he does with the left [hand].
But she danced very well. It helps when you have somebody like that in your life-
African influence.
African influence, and there were some other people . . .
Saka Eque, Bobby Crowder-
Yeah the drummers, and of course, what’s his name . . . from Nigeria, conga player Babatunde Olatunji.
Yeah, Drums of Passion.
Yeah and he had the school in Harlem when we used to go because Coltrane used to give donations for that place. Olatunji and Amy was his wife.
Is she still alive?
I think they moved to Georgia or somewhere a while back.
So Babatunde is still alive?
I don’t know.
